title: Stop negotiating with ChatGPT about diagrams

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Ever asked ChatGPT to draw a sequence diagram and gotten back half-random syntax?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Constantly. You ask for a diagram and it picks a format for you, usually the wrong one.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's exactly what annoyed Antoine. So he used AIPRM, a browser extension where the prompt template lives in the browser, and he locked four fields: diagram type, elements, purpose, and tool.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the model stops guessing whether you want PlantUML, Mermaid, or notes for Draw.io.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. It turns a diagram request into something like filling out a form instead of negotiating with the model. He even published a prompt in the AIPRM library that others can start from.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What does he use as the example?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A cached API stack. A user request goes through a React frontend to a FastAPI backend. Redis is the cache and MongoDB is the system of record. The page shows both a cache hit and a cache miss, in PlantUML and in Mermaid.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And what about canvas tools like Draw.io or Lucidchart?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Those are canvas-first, so he generates PlantUML or Mermaid first. Then he either exports it as an image to use as a baseline layer, or asks for a numbered list of lifelines and messages and rebuilds it by hand. No blank-canvas syndrome.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Two good ones. Models sometimes confuse cache-hit branches with database syntax, so always render the diagram locally before publishing. And copy the four template lines into your repo, so you're not tied to one extension version.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So he still edits the output.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: He does, but the first draft usually lands in the right language, and reviews get faster. The full write-up has the template and both code listings.
